newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU moves to adopt Basle capital adequacy rules.
newsitem.headline: EU moves to adopt Basle capital adequacy rules.

text.p: The European Commission proposed on Wednesday to allow banks and investment firms to use their own models to calculate the capital required to cover the risk involved in their activities.

The move, which is widely welcomed by banks, is a setback for securities houses trading mainly in commodities and derivatives -- mostly based in Britain -- which are currently exempt from EU capital adequacy rules altogether.

The problem is that the proposed rules, which incorporate a 1995 agreement at the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, set a single capital requirement for commodities based on the most volatile products such as oil.
Banks preferred this aproach to a complex grading of the numerous commodities traded given that this is only a marginal part of their business.
But for commodities houses the choice would be between increasing capital to match their risk exposure or develop expensive in-house risk management systems which are not available off the peg.

European commissioner Mario Monti, who is in charge of financial services, explained the proposal by the need to safeguard the stability of the financial system and provide a level playing field for all investment firms in the EU's single market.
"The amendment would ensure commodity price risks were taken fully into account when setting capital requirements," Monti said in a statement.

But to avoid disrupting the London commodities market, which accounts for some 95 percent of the EU's commodity business, the Commission proposed giving commodities houses until the end of 1999 to adapt to the new rules.

The Commission's proposal to modify the 1993 directive on capital adequacy of investment firms and credit institutions must be approved by a qualified majority of EU states and have the backing of the European Parliament.

Existing rules set a standard model for assessing risks but it is widely believed that the introduction of refined and accurate internal management models will reduce banks' capital requirements without putting the stability of the financial system at risk.
